tier_reason: The numbers are in one JSON benchmark table in a competing library's (chumsky's) README. The code is public (chumsky benches/json.rs, criterion) and the CPU is stated (Ryzen 7 3700x), but the rustc version and flags are not, so it cannot be A. A single table maintained by a competitor is not a well-known independent suite, so it is C, not B (borderline call).

corrections.claimed_speedup: winnow 178.91 us (627 MB/s) vs nom 526.52 us (213 MB/s) on chumsky's idiomatic JSON benchmark, which is ~2.9x higher throughput (derived from page data). Numbers come from the third-party table in the chumsky README, not from winnow's own docs.
corrections.caveats: Harvested from a competitor's shootout (the chumsky README), not a claim winnow makes itself; winnow's README makes no performance claims. winnow is a hard fork of nom (COPYRIGHT: 'Winnow is forked from nom'), so the baseline is its own parent. rustc version and flags are not stated; bench profile is cargo bench with debug=true. chumsky's bench (benches/json.rs, winnow 0.7 dev-dep) runs both nom 7.1 and nom 8 but the table shows a single unlabelled 'nom' row. Single JSON workload that may not generalize. GitHub reports the license as NOASSERTION, but LICENSE-MIT, Cargo.toml and COPYRIGHT all say MIT.

notes: The numbers match the table exactly. Tier moved from B to C because the source is not a well-known independent suite. The GitHub default branch was last committed 2026-09-17; the record's 2026-09-24 was pushed_at, not a default-branch commit. The chumsky repo moved to Codeberg, so benchmark_url now points there (same table).

tier_reason: This is a first-party nanobench benchmark. The code is public (benchmarks/json/ with pegtl.cpp, lexy.cpp and CMakeLists.txt) and the hardware is stated (M1 Mac Mini), but the compiler and flags are not stated on the page, so C.

corrections.caveats: First-party benchmark run by the lexy author, not an independent suite. The page states hardware (M1 Mac Mini) and harness (nanobench) but not the compiler or flags, which keeps it below A. PEGTL, nlohmann/json, rapidjson and glaze were fetched from moving branches (main/develop/master) at build time, not pinned releases. Boost.JSON is optional in CMake (find_package) and has no data series on the page. Same page, derived from its data: glaze validates ~1.5-2.3x faster than lexy on all three files; lexy is ~1.1-1.3x faster than rapidjson and ~3-9x faster than nlohmann/json.

notes: I extracted the embedded plotly data (11 samples per series). Medians match the record: canada 2.251 vs 3.649 ms, citm 1.080 vs 2.367 ms, twitter 0.749 vs 1.406 ms, lexy vs PEGTL. Metadata checks out: BSL-1.0, 1257 stars, last commit 2025-10-18 (active, just under 12 months).

tier_reason: Well-known third-party suite with public code: mariomka/regex-benchmark, nim/benchmark_regex.nim, c/benchmark.c and cpp/benchmark.cpp, driven by run-benchmarks.php. Compiler versions are in the README; flags are in run-benchmarks.php (gcc -O3 -DNDEBUG, g++ -std=c++11 -O3, nim c -d:release --opt:speed, cargo --release). Hardware: MacBook Pro 16-inch 2019 with a 2.4 GHz Core i9, no SKU number printed.

corrections.claimed_speedup: Default-settings run: nim-regex 36.09 ms total vs C PCRE2 251.37 ms (~7.0x faster) and C++ STL std::regex 1023.49 ms (~28x faster); also ~1.6x faster than default Rust regex (57.63 ms). Optimized run: nim-regex 34.15 ms vs optimized PCRE2 87.87 ms (~2.6x) and C++ STL 1021.10 ms (~30x), but optimized Rust regex (27.94 ms) beats nim-regex by ~1.2x. All ratios derived from page data.
corrections.compiler_and_flags: Nim 1.4.4, 'nim c -d:release --opt:speed' (nimble package 'regex', unpinned); C: gcc 7.5.0 -O3 -DNDEBUG with PCRE2 10.36-2; C++ STL: g++ 7.5.0 -std=c++11 -O3; Rust: rustc 1.51.0, regex 1.4.5, cargo build --release; run via Docker image mariomka/regex-benchmark:1.6
corrections.caveats: Third-party cross-language shootout (mariomka/regex-benchmark), not nim-regex's own. Results date from 2021 (Nim 1.4.4, rustc 1.51), and the nim-regex version was whatever nimble installed then. Run in Docker on macOS. The total is dominated by the Email pattern (1.32 ms vs PCRE2's 126.10 ms). In the optimized run PCRE2 beats nim-regex on IPv4 (4.73 vs 7.27 ms) and Rust beats it on URI and IPv4. The lead over PCRE2 shrinks from ~7x to ~2.6x once PCRE2 is optimized, and the Rust win only holds in the default table. The std::regex comparison is libstdc++ (g++ 7.5.0) only.

notes: Every number matches the README rows for Nim Regex, C PCRE2, Rust and C++ STL. I confirmed the 'Nim Regex' row is nitely's package: Dockerfile runs 'nimble install regex'. Compiler flags come from run-benchmarks.php, not the README.

tier_reason: The project's own JMH suite is public (safere-benchmarks/, run-java-benchmarks.sh, raw results under benchmark-results/published/516a1ff...). BENCHMARKS.md states OpenJDK 26.0.2 with JMH settings, g++ 13.3.0 -O3 -DNDEBUG for native RE2, and CPU i7-11700K, against java.util.regex, so A.

corrections.claimed_speedup: Geometric mean 2.22x faster than JDK java.util.regex on the 150-row real-world matrix (1.88x without the 2 pathological backtracking rows), but 22% slower than JDK on Core and 7% slower on Application. 12.5x faster than RE2/J and 3.06x faster than RE2-FFM on the real-world matrix. Against native engines on the real-world matrix, SafeRE is 13% slower than C++ RE2 (150 rows), takes 2.03x as long as Rust regex (150 rows) and 2.47x as long as PCRE2 JIT (only 48 supported rows). It is 1.32x faster than native RE2 on Core.

notes: Numbers match BENCHMARKS.md. I fixed one inaccuracy: the PCRE2 JIT ratio covers 48 supported rows, not the full 150-row matrix. The license is BSD-3-Clause (pom.xml declares it; GitHub shows NOASSERTION because LICENSE bundles the RE2 and RE2/J notices), and the GPL OpenJDK-derived suite lives in a separate repo. It is a mixed result that only beats the JDK incumbent, which is not on the list.
